title: NewHope & Saber — Noise vs Rounding in Lattice KEMs

questions.question: In the ring R_q = Z_q[x]/(x^n + 1), what does the relation x^n = -1 mean for multiplication?
options: High-degree terms wrap around with a minus sign (negacyclic reduction).
Polynomials become cyclic: x^n = 1 so terms wrap without sign changes.
All coefficients must be either 0 or 1 after reduction.
Multiplication is undefined unless q is prime.
questions.explanation: Reducing modulo (x^n+1) implies x^n ≡ -1, so x^{n+k} ≡ -x^k and overflowed terms subtract back in.

questions.question: In LWE-style constructions, why do we add an error term e in b = a·s + e (mod q)?
options: It hides the secret by making the relation noisy, which is the source of hardness.
It prevents the need for a random public a, so a can be constant.
It makes decryption deterministic with no chance of failure.
It allows replacing multiplication with addition.
questions.explanation: Without error, the system becomes exact linear equations; with error, distinguishing/recovering secrets is conjectured hard.

questions.question: In the toy RLWE PKE, why does `encode_bits_as_poly` map a bit 1 to q//2 (instead of 1)?
options: Because after adding small noise, coefficients stay near either 0 or q/2, enabling threshold decoding by distance.
Because q//2 is always a primitive root of unity needed for NTT.
Because it makes ciphertexts smaller by half.
Because it removes the need for randomness in encryption.
questions.explanation: The decoder chooses whichever center (0 or q/2) is closer; embedding far apart gives robustness to noise.

questions.question: What is the key conceptual difference between RLWE (NewHope flavor) and RLWR/LWR (Saber flavor)?
options: RLWE uses sampled random error; LWR gets its effective error from deterministic rounding (dropping bits).
RLWE is symmetric-key only; LWR is public-key only.
RLWE can’t use polynomial rings; LWR can.
RLWE always uses power-of-two moduli; LWR always uses primes.
questions.explanation: LWR replaces explicit error sampling with information loss from mapping Z_q to a smaller Z_p via rounding.

questions.question: When p divides q, what does `poly_round_to_p` compute for a coefficient x in Z_q?
options: The nearest element in Z_p to (p/q)·x (implemented as add-half-then-divide).
A cryptographic hash of x reduced mod p.
The lowest log2(p) bits of x.
A random element of Z_p derived from x.
questions.explanation: With scale=q/p, rounding is approximately ⌊(x + scale/2)/scale⌋ mod p, i.e., quantizing x into p buckets.

questions.question: Why is domain separation important when using an XOF to derive values like a, s, e, and r from seeds?
options: To ensure different roles produce independent streams even if a seed is reused.
To make the output shorter so keys are smaller.
To force all outputs to be uniformly random without rejection sampling.
To make decoding always succeed regardless of noise.
questions.explanation: Using different domain tags avoids accidental correlations (or catastrophic reuse) between values meant to be independent.

questions.question: Attack intuition: what is a major risk if you set the RLWE error distribution to zero (no e, no e') in a = uniform, b = a·s (mod q)?
options: The public key becomes an exact equation that can often be solved with linear algebra to recover s.
Ciphertexts become larger and slower but remain secure.
Decryption becomes impossible because noise is required to decode.
It forces you to switch to LWR because RLWE requires errors.
questions.explanation: Removing noise collapses the hardness assumption: the attacker sees exact algebraic relations instead of noisy ones.

questions.question: Why do real lattice KEMs typically apply a Fujisaki–Okamoto (FO) style transform on top of an IND-CPA PKE?
options: To upgrade to chosen-ciphertext security by re-encrypting/checking and binding the ciphertext into key derivation.
To remove the need for randomness in encryption.
To turn a KEM into a signature scheme.
To avoid polynomial multiplication.
questions.explanation: FO-style transforms are the standard way to obtain IND-CCA security from a CPA-secure lattice PKE in the random oracle model.
